beat: Year one. His idea. It rained the whole way up and he called it perfect: "nobody else gets the view when it rains."
lines: His idea, the first one. He had it in a kebab shop at one in the morning.
It rained from the car park to the top.
You said something about turning back. He kept walking.
There was no view up there at all, just white, and he called it perfect. Nobody else gets the view when it rains.
You took the photo to make him stop talking.

beat: Nobody wants to play keeper. He raised his hand every single week like it was an honor.
lines: Nobody wants to go in goal.
Every Wednesday, eleven grown men studying their own shoes, and his hand already up.
He was not good. He was enthusiastic, which is a different thing and much louder.
He kept the bib in his own bag so the job could never be given to anyone else.

beat: The naming ceremony. He watered it with a wine glass because "Zlatan deserves stemware."
lines: The naming took forty minutes and involved a shortlist.
You argued for something ordinary. You lost, on the grounds that ordinary plants die.
He watered it out of a wine glass that first night, because Zlatan deserves stemware.
Every green thing he owned before this one died. He never mentioned them again, out of respect.

beat: The co-op save at 83%. You were saving the last level "for a good night."
lines: Eighty-three percent, and his save slot named so that nobody could delete it by accident.
You were saving the last level for a good night.
There was no shortage of good nights. That was never the problem.
You assumed there would be another one. Everyone assumes that. It is how a week gets made.

beat: The war with the fridge, dramatized. He lost for years. The towel was his masterpiece.
lines: The fridge hummed in a key he described, seriously, as hostile.
Two years of shims. A folded envelope. A paperback he had not enjoyed.
Then the towel, quartered, wedged under the front left corner.
He called you at eleven at night to listen to nothing. You listened to nothing for a full minute. Best call of that year.

beat: You chipped it the first month he lived here. He declared it legally yours at a small ceremony.
lines: You chipped it on the tap, first month he lived here.
There was a ceremony. There was a speech. The speech was deliberately too long.
From then on it was your mug, and guests were informed.
He never drank from it again. It was yours, and he was strict about it.

beat: Shortest fragment. Smell is the fastest road back. One image: him late, jogging to meet you, smelling like this.
lines: He is late.
He is jogging up the street with his coat open, apologising before he is close enough to be heard.
He smells like this.

beat: He didn't smoke. He carried his father's fire in his pocket for eight years and lit other people's birthdays with it.
lines: He never smoked a day in his life.
He carried it for eight years anyway. Right-hand pocket, always the right-hand pocket.
Other people's candles. Other people's cigarettes, outside, in the cold, while he stood there not smoking.
You never asked him about it. It seemed like the kind of thing you did not ask about.

beat: The hospital, age 19. Him printing your name in the emergency contact line: "so Mum never gets a call like that again." You signed witness like it was nothing. It was not nothing.
lines: The hospital, the year his father died. A clipboard, a biro on a string.
He printed your name into the emergency contact line without asking whether you minded.
So Mum never gets a call like that again.
You signed underneath as the witness, in the corridor, standing up.
You were nineteen. It took four seconds. You did not think about it once in eight years, and then you thought about nothing else.

beat: Low Orbit's one real gig. The broken string mid-set, and him finishing the song anyway, laughing, on three strings.
lines: One real gig. Forty people, most of them related to somebody on stage.
The string went in the second song. You heard it go from the back of the room.
He finished on three, laughing, and not one person out there could tell.
Tomi still says they were tight that night. Tomi was and remains a liar.

beat: Summer nights out here. The time he leaned back too far and grabbed the string lights and they held. The whole street heard you both.
lines: Summer. Both chairs out, the door propped open with a boot.
He tipped his chair back one time too many and caught the lights on the way.
They held. Of course they held. He had put them up himself, with a great deal more hardware than the job needed.
You both made a noise the whole street heard. Somebody applauded from two floors down.

beat: Eight envelopes in your handwriting. What you told everyone. What you were actually buying: a door that stayed closed. Text 7.8.
lines: Eight envelopes. Your handwriting on every one of them.
You told Lena the landlord was being flexible. You told Mr. Rako you were handling the estate.
You told yourself it was practical, and practical is an excellent place to keep something you would rather not look at.
What you were buying, every month, on time, was a door that stayed shut.
